newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seeks revived budget talks, Hill skeptical.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seeks revived budget talks, Hill skeptical.

text.p: With Republican squabbles over tax cuts giving him an opening, President Clinton sought Wednesday to revive talks on balancing the federal budget, which had seemed doomed by partisan differences.
Clinton invited leaders of congressional budget committees to the White House for a 2:30 p.m. parley to resuscitate negotiations on eliminating the federal deficit by 2002.

But the Senate's leading Republican, Trent Lott of Mississippi, spoke disparagingly of the meeting before it started, indicating he thought the White House was engaging in public relations while forgoing real chances for agreement.

"I don't think a lot will come out of that," Lott, who was not expected to attend the meeting, told reporters. "I don't think we're going to have a big event, you know, or something substantive come out of a show-and-tell."
The White House said Clinton would speak to a small group of reporters at 4 p.m. EST about the meeting.

Almost everyone in Washington voices support for balancing the budget, but there has been little progress toward the goal. Clinton saw a chance for movement this week when House Speaker Newt Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, suddenly suggested shelving big tax cuts that Democrats opposed.

The president asked for Wednesday's meeting because "there were some significant things said by the (Republican congressional) leadership this week and he wanted to respond to that," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.

Acknowledging the storm of protest Gingrich's comments provoked among conservative Republicans devoted to a tax cut, McCurry said, "the Republicans are coming to grips with themselves on some of these issues internally and ... we want to understand better what the feelings are in their caucus."

But Lott said he felt Clinton missed a big opportunity to balance the budget by reducing the consumer price index, which is used to calculate the cost of living and thus many federal benefit programmes such as Social Security for retirees. Lott had joined those who endorsed an expert commission on the issue, but Clinton did not.

"I stuck my neck out there on the CPI, nothing happened there," Lott said. He said it was possible to craft a five-year balanced budget agreement without a CPI change, "but it makes it much more difficult."

He suggested Clinton had caved in to Democrats who oppose the CPI change, including House Minority Leader Richard Gephardt of Missouri. "They can see full well that Dick Gephardt and his allies in the union movement would be ginning up television spots blasting people on the change in the CPI," Lott said.
Meanwhile top House Republicans repeated their commitment to cutting taxes but said they did not know how they would move procedurally to make this happen.

"The Republican party continues to stand for lower taxes for all Americans," Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich said after a meeting of House Republicans. The Ohio Republican suggested splitting the budget into smaller bills.
"We'd like to take one major piece of this balanced budget and get it signed into law," such as a deal on Medicare health care spending for the elderly, Kasich said.

He and House Majority Whip Tom DeLay, a Texas Republican, would not say how big a tax cut they wanted. Senate Republicans have called for about $200 billion in reductions over five years, about twice the level in Clinton's balanced budget plan.

Gingrich's views on taxes differed sharply from those of some other Republicans including 28 conservatives who warned in a letter to House Republican leaders Tuesday that a postponement could doom chances for winning the tax cuts.
"Rather than folding, some members ought to exercise leadership, drive a message and fight for a principle," the group's leader, Representative David McIntosh of Indiana, said.

Lott said Republicans should develop their own budget plan, possibly working with conservative Democrats. "I no longer think we can afford to delay our own actions and our own preparations in producing a budget in expectation that something will happen with the administration," he said.
